summary: The machine has the essential pieces to start building the Python + LangChain + Beanie sample against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster: python, docker, the documentdb MCP server, the azure MCP server and Microsoft Learn search, plus a broad set of documentdb-* agent skills. Most cold-answer facts were verifiable and several were partially outdated because this product exposes a dedicated mongoClusters resource (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) that is distinct from older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts-based Mongo API accounts. Missing developer conveniences (mongosh, azd, bicep/terraform) and an unspecified embedding/LLM choice are the main gaps but each has an available workaround so the build can proceed.
summary_points: All required data-plane tools for inspecting and verifying the live cluster are present: the documentdb MCP server is available and offers index/collection/query tools; Microsoft Learn search (learn) is available for fact-checking.

Python 3.13 is installed and the DocumentDB agent skills (connection, vector-search, driver, local-deploy, etc.) are present, so app code using motor + Beanie can be written and reviewed with skill guidance.

Several cold answers incorrectly described the older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts/Mongo API model rather than the current dedicated mongoClusters resource (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters); use the mongoClusters docs for deployment, CLI and connection-string details.

Key missing accelerators / CLI tools that would speed iterative verification: mongosh (for ad-hoc DB inspection) and azd/bicep/terraform (if the builder wanted to provision infra). They are not required for the sample because a live cluster is already provided.

Missing design details that matter to code: embedding model name and vector dimension, which determine vector-index parameters and sample-data embedding generation; the sample must pick and document these decisions.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (API for MongoDB is created as a databaseAccount with kind or capabilities set to MongoDB).
confusions.grounded_answer: The dedicated managed Mongo cluster resource uses the provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB with the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts) for the vCore/dedicated Mongo cluster offering.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace and historical overlap: older Cosmos DB Mongo API used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the new dedicated Mongo cluster resource is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. The two resource types are in the same provider namespace which causes mix-ups.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep or targeted CLI commands for databaseAccounts, they would either attempt to operate on the wrong resource type or fail to find the dedicated mongo-cluster resource; IaC and CLI commands would be incorrect.
improvements: Add a prominent note on the 'Quickstart' and 'Overview' pages clarifying that 'mongoClusters' is the dedicated vCore cluster resource and not the 'databaseAccounts' resource used by the Cosmos Mongo API.
Update any guidance in the agent kit to prefer Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters when the sample target is a dedicated vCore Mongo cluster.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create -g MyRG -n my-docdb-account --kind MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Current CLI uses dedicated command groups for mongo cluster resources: az cosmosdb mongocluster (and az documentdb mongocluster) provide create/show/list operations for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. The commands are present in the core az CLI command groups (the cosmosdb/documentdb command modules), with some subcommands marked preview. There is also a documentdb command group alias in some docs.

grounding_links.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create
az documentdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically 'az cosmosdb' operated on databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB; dedicated mongo cluster subcommands were added and docs sometimes provide both 'az cosmosdb' and 'az documentdb' forms, leading to ambiguity.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create with databaseAccounts syntax will create or target a Cosmos DB account rather than a dedicated mongoClusters resource; CLI commands and parameters (ports, auth modes) will differ and the builder may fail to create the intended resource.
improvements: Document the preferred az subcommand (az cosmosdb mongocluster or az documentdb mongocluster) on the quickstarts and in the agent-kit CLI examples.
Add a single canonical example in the sample README that shows the exact az mongocluster create command to use when provisioning (or note that provisioning is out-of-scope for this sample).

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For the dedicated vCore MongoDB cluster the correct resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (use the mongoClusters ARM/Bicep resource and the corresponding terraform/AzAPI module or AVM documented for the 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' mongo-cluster resource). databaseAccounts (azurerm_cosmosdb_account) is the older Cosmos account resource class and not the dedicated mongo cluster resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The provider namespace is the same and past guidance for 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB' used databaseAccounts; the newer dedicated mongoClusters resource was introduced and is documented separately.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder used ARM/Bicep templates for databaseAccounts, they might attempt to create the wrong resource type; Terraform modules would target the wrong provider resource and the created resource would not expose dedicated mongo-cluster features (vCore, node tiers).
improvements: Add a clear migration/renaming note on the databaseAccounts template page and link to mongoClusters so authors know which resource type to use for vCore clusters.
Include a mongoClusters Bicep snippet in the agent kit sample repo for quick copy-paste.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos DB (Mongo API) connection string looks like: mongodb://<USER>:<PASS>@<ACCOUNT>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For dedicated mongoClusters the cluster typically exposes Mongo-compatible endpoints like mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster-name>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/ or mongodb://<host>:<port> with TLS (tls=true), SCRAM auth and provider-specific connection-string variants; the older databaseAccounts/Cosmos-hosted strings used .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255 — that describes the Cosmos DB databaseAccounts Mongo API, not the dedicated mongoClusters endpoint. Obtain the exact connection string from the cluster Connection strings page; dedicated clusters commonly use SRV records under *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and the sample should read the full URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell
Get cluster connection strings (PowerShell/SDK docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (older Mongo API) and dedicated mongoClusters expose Mongo-style URIs but hostnames, ports and required options differ; the cold answer described the Cosmos databaseAccounts pattern (10255 and replicaSet=globaldb).

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) Mongo connection format (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding 10255 and Cosmos-specific options (replicaSet=globaldb) could lead to connection failures or insecure assumptions when the sample runs against a dedicated mongoClusters endpoint. The sample must read a provided DOCUMENTDB_URI and use it unchanged.
improvements: In sample README and agent kit example code, show how to read DOCUMENTDB_URI from environment and avoid constructing connection strings by hand.
Add a short 'Connection string differences' note on the Connect quickstart that lists the SRV host pattern for mongoClusters vs the older .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 pattern.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB supports RU/s or serverless; for Mongo you can also choose dedicated vCore-based MongoDB clusters (instance tiers like M10/M30) — billed by compute (vCore/instance size) and storage.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the dedicated managed Mongo/vCore offering) uses dedicated node/sku compute tiers (e.g., M-series like M30) and is billed by compute/storage (vCore-style tiers). RU/s throughput is the Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) model. The two are distinct billing models and the sample's cluster (M30 vCore) is a vCore-tiered cluster.

grounding_links.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) cluster (mongoClusters) README / usage examples
Azure DocumentDB FAQ explaining vCore/vs RU differences

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (Mongo API) and the dedicated vCore offering provide Mongo-compatible interfaces; they use different billing models and historically guidance blended both.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB 'Estimate RU' pages (still relevant when using databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Choosing index / cluster sizing or cost estimates using RU/s rather than node-vCore pricing will give wrong guidance for the M30 cluster and might lead to mis-sized demos or confusing README guidance.
improvements: Clarify 'billing model' on quickstart and sample README: explicitly state whether the sample targets a vCore (mongoClusters) or RU (databaseAccounts) resource and link to pricing docs.
Agent kit templates should include a short checklist: 'Is this a vCore cluster (mongoClusters) or a databaseAccounts Mongo API account?' and change sample code accordingly.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth for the MongoDB API is Mongo-style credentials (SCRAM); AAD auth is supported for Cosmos DB via Azure SDKs; AAD not generally available for raw Mongo drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Dedicated mongoClusters support both native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (MicrosoftEntraID) as an allowed auth mode on the cluster (the CLI docs expose --auth-allowed-modes NativeAuth MicrosoftEntraID). The cluster can provide connection strings for native or Entra ID flows; if using AAD, you typically obtain an AAD token (via az/login or MSAL) and use provider-specific instructions — the cluster docs show Microsoft Entra ID as an available auth mode.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (auth-allowed-modes option)
Enable private access & get connection string guidance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API primarily used SCRAM credentials and Azure SDKs exposed AAD flows for the SQL API; newer dedicated clusters added Microsoft Entra ID modes which authors might not expect.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB documentation describing AAD support for some APIs (SQL/core)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM creds are supported, they may skip implementing the AAD credential path required if the cluster is configured to require or allow Microsoft Entra ID; conversely, coding for AAD when the cluster only allows native auth will also fail.
improvements: Add an auth-mode subsection in the quickstart explaining how to detect whether MicrosoftEntraID is enabled (portal/CLI) and how to get the correct connection string for the chosen auth mode.
Agent kit samples should include small code snippets for both native (SCRAM) and AAD token flows and show how to select at runtime based on cluster configuration.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For MongoDB-compatible workloads use the official MongoDB drivers (pymongo/motor); azure-cosmos is for SQL/core API and not correct for Mongo workloads.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for synchronous, motor for async) and ODMs that build on them (Beanie uses motor). There is not a separate service-specific Python SDK for the Mongo wire protocol; azure-cosmos targets SQL/Core API only.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-driver
Use motor + Beanie example guidance

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: On MongoDB 7.0-style vector support you typically see indexes like HNSW, IVF or DiskANN. Representative create-index command with embedding: method 'hnsw' and options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports DiskANN, HNSW and IVF indexing methods. Index creation is performed through the createIndexes command or provider-specific createIndex variant and uses provider options (e.g., cosmosSearchOptions with kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and dimensions, similarity, and tuning parameters). The product docs provide JSON templates and language-specific snippets to create HNSW/IVF/DiskANN vector indexes and use the $search stage with the cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN examples)
create a vector index example (cosmosSearchOptions / kind vector-ivf)

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text for Cosmos DB is done with Azure Cognitive Search or by using text indexes; hybrid is achieved by external vector-capable search (Azure Cognitive Search) or app-side re-ranking.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides an integrated search capability that supports lexical (text) search and vector search together via the $search aggregation stage and the cosmosSearch operator — you can create text-like indexes and vector indexes and perform hybrid queries (vector search plus filter/lexical scoring) without an external Azure Cognitive Search service. Azure Cognitive Search remains an option for some scenarios, but it is not required for hybrid vector+text search in Azure DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (hybrid search and $search/cosmosSearch operator)
Use LangChain on Azure with Azure DocumentDB (vector index creation examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos patterns and external integrations (Azure Cognitive Search) are common and documentation historically emphasized Azure Search for full-text; the Product now exposes integrated hybrid search primitives (cosmosSearch) that unify vector and text.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos integration guidance (older hybrid patterns)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder designs the sample around an external Cognitive Search pipeline, they add extra moving parts and unnecessary ETL instead of using the built-in $search/cosmosSearch capabilities; that will complicate the sample and increase cost.
improvements: Update the quickstart to show a single integrated example (create vector index + $search pipeline) and mention Azure Cognitive Search only as an alternative for scenarios requiring its feature set.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported versions depend on account; historically Cosmos offered 3.6/4.0/4.2 and more recent may advertise 5.x/6.x/7.0. Some features (server-side JS, oplog control, certain newer operators) may be missing; change-stream support varies.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB server-version compatibility up to modern versions (serverVersion options include 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and newer in docs) depending on cluster configuration. Some MongoDB features can differ; the compatibility reference and feature matrix must be consulted for specific operators and aggregation stages. The sample must test any advanced features against the target cluster.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts ApiProperties serverVersion values (3.2..7.0)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (compatibility notes)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Services and compatibility evolve; older docs referenced older MongoDB versions and some posts mix Atlas/server behavior vs managed platform behavior.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API versioning docs

confusions.build_risk: Assuming support for a specific MongoDB feature (e.g., a particular aggregation stage or server-side JS) without testing against the target cluster may cause runtime failures in the sample.
improvements: Add explicit compatibility-check command snippets to the sample README (e.g., run an explain or a small pipeline) and reference the compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Cosmos DB Emulator for SQL API; for Mongo API run a local MongoDB container on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development the recommended local gateway image is the DocumentDB Gateway container (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) which exposes the Mongo wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). The Cosmos DB emulator does not fully support the Mongo API. Running a stock Mongo container is a useful fallback but will not exactly match the DocumentDB engine's behavior. The documentdb-local-deployment skill documents using the Gateway image and port 10260 for local development.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Quickstart: Use vector search with Python in Azure DocumentDB (local tips)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: General Mongo development often uses a stock Mongo container on 27017; older Cosmos emulator guidance applies to SQL/core API and not Mongo. The DocumentDB project provides a specific local gateway on different ports.
confusions.build_risk: If tests are written against a stock Mongo container on 27017 they may pass locally but fail against DocumentDB due to subtle behavioral differences; recommended to include a note and scripts that either use the DocumentDB gateway image or mark tests as integration-only.
improvements: Add a short example docker-compose.yml and docker run command using the documented gateway image and port 10260 to the sample README.
Document the behavior differences and advise running integration tests against the live cluster for final verification.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Support depends on account and MongoDB compatibility version; earlier Cosmos offerings did not always support change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. For some multishard clusters an additional 'Change streams for multishard clusters' preview feature may need to be enabled in cluster settings; the docs explain enabling change-stream related features and using Model.watch()/watch() APIs. Online migrations and triggers depend on change streams. The product docs include a 'Change streams' page with examples and feature notes.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Mongoose on Azure DocumentDB (Model.watch uses change streams and notes on enabling multishard change-stream preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Change stream support depended historically on account type and version; docs must be checked per-cluster. The cold answer hedged correctly but understated that the feature exists and may need explicit enabling.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses change streams (e.g., audit agents) without checking cluster settings, it may fail; the sample should verify change-stream availability and enable the preview feature in the cluster if required.
improvements: Add a small startup check in the sample that attempts to open a change stream and surfaces a clear error message with instructions if the cluster needs the change-stream feature enabled.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The documentdb-specific MCP server (named documentdb) provides data-plane inspection and tools; the general azure MCP server covers control-plane but not the full data-plane.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the environment provides a 'documentdb' MCP server that exposes data-plane tools (list databases, find documents, index creation, explain, aggregate). The general azure MCP server is available for control-plane and documentation lookups but does not replace the documentdb data-plane tools.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally launched Azure DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; Azure DocumentDB (historic name) is not the same as open-source project DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly historic truth but currently confusing: the Azure brand has reused the 'DocumentDB' name. Historically Azure DocumentDB became Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB API). Separately, Microsoft now ships a managed MongoDB-compatible offering called Azure DocumentDB (aligned with the open-source DocumentDB engine) which is distinct from the old DocumentDB->Cosmos lineage. The naming overlap causes confusion; docs explicitly describe the relationship and warn about the name re-use.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB FAQ — relationship to Cosmos and DocumentDB engine

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' has been reused historically and for different products, causing ambiguity between the old DocumentDB (which became Cosmos DB) and the new Azure DocumentDB managed Mongo product built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.

confusion_sources.title: Blog posts and older docs referencing DocumentDB and Cosmos migration

confusions.build_risk: Builders may mistakenly follow old Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) quickstarts and APIs when the sample must target the dedicated mongoClusters offering; naming confusion could cause them to pick the wrong ARM resources or CLI commands.
improvements: Add a short 'Which DocumentDB are we talking about?' note in the agent kit and sample README that explicitly states 'This sample targets the vCore-based Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) offering — not the historical DocumentDB that became Azure Cosmos DB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the service is an emulation layer on top of the Cosmos DB engine or on a managed MongoDB engine; from application code use the Mongo driver but test features.
confusions.grounded_answer: The dedicated Azure DocumentDB offering is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (not MongoDB server), and it presents the MongoDB wire protocol to clients. That means standard drivers should work for most operations but there are compatibility differences (index semantics, some aggregation/ops) that must be tested. The sample should use standard Mongo drivers and validate any advanced Mongo features it relies on against the actual cluster.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB FAQ and engine details
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (engine & compatibility notes)

confusions.cold_answer: Use motor as the transport, pymongo-compatible URI, and Beanie ODM on top; client = motor.AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) then Beanie.init_beanie(...).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and supported: use motor (async driver) + Beanie. The documentdb-driver skill and local-deploy docs give patterns for singleton AsyncIOMotorClient and Beanie initialization.

confusions.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for embedding search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with HNSW parameters: db.profiles.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine', M: 16, efConstruction: 200 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: Partially correct conceptually (HNSW is supported) but the vendor-specific DocumentDB API prefers createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions (kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann') and explicit fields such as dimensions and similarity. Also the index dimensions must match the chosen embedding model (the sample must pick a model — e.g., 1536 for many OpenAI/third-party models — and use that dimension).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (createIndexes examples and cosmosSearchOptions)
Create vector index examples (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF via SDK/commands)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic MongoDB 7.0 'createIndex vector' syntax; DocumentDB uses provider-specific createIndexes/create_index payloads (cosmosSearchOptions) and often a SRV endpoint. Also embedding dimension is determined by external embedding model which the cold answer assumed.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to run the Mongo-style createIndex with vendor-incompatible options will fail; using the wrong dimension (not matching embedding model) will create a misconfigured index.
improvements: In the sample README state: 'Pick an embedding model and its vector dimension (e.g., text-embedding-3-small -> 1536) and use the DocumentDB createIndexes payload with cosmosSearchOptions.kind set to the chosen index type (hnsw/ivf/diskann). Provide the exact createIndexes JSON we intend to run.'

confusions.question: What collections and indexes will the sample create?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections: profiles, golden_records, audit_logs. Indexes: vector index on profiles.embedding, text index on name and bio, unique index on golden_records._id.
confusions.grounded_answer: Conceptually correct naming and index plan: the sample should create profiles (with vector embeddings and filterable fields), golden_records and audit_logs. The exact index creation calls must use DocumentDB's createIndexes API (cosmosSearchOptions for vector indexes) and Mongo text/index semantics for text fields; also create filter indexes for prefiltering (email, phone). The sample must ensure index definitions align with the chosen embedding dimension and cluster tier.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-vector-search
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (indexing guidance and mixed filters)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is a reasonable suggested plan but omitted the DocumentDB-specific createIndexes payload and the requirement to match vector dimensions to the embedding model.
confusions.build_risk: If indexes are created incorrectly or with wrong dims, vector search will fail or return empty results. Missing filter indexes will make prefiltering inefficient.
improvements: Add concrete createIndexes examples (JSON/driver calls) to the sample repository for the exact cluster API the builder will execute, and document the expected embedding dimension.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and vector dimension
information_gaps.description: The sample requires a concrete choice of embedding model (provider and model name) because the vector index dimensions and similarity assumptions (COS vs L2) depend on this. I searched Microsoft Learn and the skill docs (documentdb-vector-search) and found guidance on how to create vector indexes but the sample prompt did not specify which embedding model to use.

information_gaps.title: LLM/chat provider and credentials
information_gaps.description: The prompt requests "LLM-assisted similarity scoring" but does not specify which LLM/chat provider or environment variables to use for API keys (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.). I looked through the prompt, prompt_review and installed skills; none prescribe the provider or env var names for LLMs.

information_gaps.title: Sample dataset schema/seed data
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for profile documents but gives no sample data, counts, or a seed script. The documentdb-local-deployment skill suggests seed script patterns but no concrete sample dataset was provided.

information_gaps.title: Exact createIndexes payload to run in the sample
information_gaps.description: DocumentDB uses createIndexes with provider-specific options (cosmosSearchOptions / kind keys). The cold answers show examples but the sample must have an exact JSON snippet for the specific cluster API version to avoid runtime errors. I reviewed the vector-search docs but the exact payload depends on chosen index kind and dimension, which is not specified.

information_gaps.title: Run/test matrix (mocked vs live)
information_gaps.description: The prompt expects verification against a live cluster. There is no guidance about which unit tests must run offline (mocks) and which integration tests require the live cluster, nor provided mocking fixtures. The installed skills do not include a test harness for offline unit tests.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) and the az cosmosdb mongocluster or az documentdb mongocluster CLI group when you need to reference or provision a dedicated vCore Mongo cluster; see the mongoClusters ARM/Bicep docs.

Read the complete connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime (do not hardcode ports or host suffixes); for dedicated clusters prefer the cluster-provided SRV or host connection string shown in the portal.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

guidance_for_builder.instruction: When creating vector indexes, pick an embedding model first and set the index 'dimensions' to that model's output size; create the vector index using DocumentDB's createIndexes payload (cosmosSearchOptions kind = 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann') as shown in the vector-search docs.

sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (createIndexes examples)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use motor + Beanie for async Python code and follow the documentdb-driver skill patterns (singleton AsyncIOMotorClient, reuse client across coroutines, and call Beanie.init_beanie once during startup).

Verify change-stream usage at startup (attempt to open a short-lived change stream or query cluster capabilities) and surface a clear error message if the cluster requires enabling the multishard change-stream preview feature.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH (recommended) for quick interactive checks of indexes and queries; simplest installation is to follow MongoDB's official mongosh install docs for the platform. If not installed, rely on the documentdb MCP server's list_indexes/find_documents/explain calls for verification.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: azd (Azure Developer CLI) is useful for templated dev-to-cloud workflows but the sample environment provides a live cluster and az CLI; add azd only if you plan to add IaC-based provisioning or developer scaffolding. Not required to build this sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is useful if authors want to include Bicep templates to provision resources. The run policy forbids provisioning new clusters for this sample so it's optional; if needed, install Bicep on PATH or use 'az deployment' with inline templates.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform helps if the builder wants to ship Terraform examples; not required because the live cluster is provided. If desired, install terraform or use AzAPI provider templates in CI.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Dotnet is unnecessary for a Python sample; ignore unless you plan to generate .NET companion samples.
